claim: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria (HGPS) is a premature ageing syndrome caused by a mutation in LMNA, resulting in a truncated form of lamin A called progerin.
source: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria (HGPS) is a premature ageing syndrome caused by a mutation in LMNA, resulting in a truncated form of lamin A called progerin.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about HGPS supported by scientific consensus and citations in the introduction.

claim: Progerin triggers loss of the heterochromatic marker H3K27me3.
source: Progerin triggers loss of the heterochromatic marker H3K27me3, and premature senescence, which is prevented by telomerase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F demonstrating inverse correlation between progerin and H3K27me3 levels.

claim: Progerin triggers premature senescence, which is prevented by telomerase.
source: Progerin triggers loss of the heterochromatic marker H3K27me3, and premature senescence, which is prevented by telomerase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G showing reduced senescence-associated β-gal-positive cells with TERT expression.

claim: LAP2α (lamina-associated polypeptide-α) interacts with lamin A.
source: Here, we describe an inducible cellular system to model HGPS and find that LAP2α (lamina-associated polypeptide-α) interacts with lamin A, while its interaction with progerin is significantly reduced.
evidence: This is supported by BioID analysis (Figure 3C) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3D).

claim: The interaction between LAP2α and progerin is significantly reduced compared to lamin A.
source: Here, we describe an inducible cellular system to model HGPS and find that LAP2α (lamina-associated polypeptide-α) interacts with lamin A, while its interaction with progerin is significantly reduced.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BioID mass spectrometry (Figure 3C) and co-immunoprecipitation showing 40-60% less LAP2α pulled down by progerin (Figure 3D).

claim: Over 50% of telomeres localize to the lamina.
source: Super-resolution microscopy revealed that over 50% of telomeres localize to the lamina and that LAP2α association with telomeres is impaired in HGPS.
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: LAP2α association with telomeres is impaired in HGPS.
source: Super-resolution microscopy revealed that over 50% of telomeres localize to the lamina and that LAP2α association with telomeres is impaired in HGPS.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3D-SIM microscopy showing altered LAP2α distribution profile around telomeres in HGPS cells (Figure 4D).

claim: Increasing LAP2α levels rescues progerin-induced proliferation defects.
source: This impaired interaction is central to HGPS since increasing LAP2α levels rescues progerin-induced proliferation defects and loss of H3K27me3, whereas lowering LAP2 levels exacerbates progerin-induced defects.
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5C showing restored proliferation upon LAP2α induction.

claim: Increasing LAP2α levels rescues progerin-induced loss of H3K27me3.
source: This impaired interaction is central to HGPS since increasing LAP2α levels rescues progerin-induced proliferation defects and loss of H3K27me3, whereas lowering LAP2 levels exacerbates progerin-induced defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5F and 5G showing increased H3K27me3 levels upon LAP2α expression.

claim: Lowering LAP2 levels exacerbates progerin-induced defects.
source: This impaired interaction is central to HGPS since increasing LAP2α levels rescues progerin-induced proliferation defects and loss of H3K27me3, whereas lowering LAP2 levels exacerbates progerin-induced defects.
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5A showing enhanced proliferation defects in LAP2-depleted cells expressing progerin.

claim: HGPS is caused by an autosomal dominant C to T nucleotide substitution at position 1824 (G608G) in LMNA.
source: HGPS is caused by an autosomal dominant C to T nucleotide substitution at position 1824 (G608G) in LMNA, which activates a cryptic splice site and results in a truncated and constitutively farnesylated version of lamin A called progerin (De Sandre-Giovannoli et al., 2003; Eriksson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The G608G mutation activates a cryptic splice site and results in a truncated and constitutively farnesylated version of lamin A called progerin.
source: HGPS is caused by an autosomal dominant C to T nucleotide substitution at position 1824 (G608G) in LMNA, which activates a cryptic splice site and results in a truncated and constitutively farnesylated version of lamin A called progerin (De Sandre-Giovannoli et al., 2003; Eriksson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: HGPS fibroblasts have a greatly reduced proliferative capacity.
source: HGPS fibroblasts have a greatly reduced proliferative capacity, abnormal nuclear architecture, persistent activation of DNA damage checkpoints and shortened telomeres (Allsopp et al., 1992; Bridger and Kill, 2004; Goldman et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2005, 2006; Decker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and confirmed by experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: HGPS fibroblasts have abnormal nuclear architecture.
source: HGPS fibroblasts have a greatly reduced proliferative capacity, abnormal nuclear architecture, persistent activation of DNA damage checkpoints and shortened telomeres (Allsopp et al., 1992; Bridger and Kill, 2004; Goldman et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2005, 2006; Decker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and confirmed by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HGPS fibroblasts have persistent activation of DNA damage checkpoints.
source: HGPS fibroblasts have a greatly reduced proliferative capacity, abnormal nuclear architecture, persistent activation of DNA damage checkpoints and shortened telomeres (Allsopp et al., 1992; Bridger and Kill, 2004; Goldman et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2005, 2006; Decker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and confirmed by 53BP1 foci data in Figure 1D.

claim: HGPS fibroblasts have shortened telomeres.
source: HGPS fibroblasts have a greatly reduced proliferative capacity, abnormal nuclear architecture, persistent activation of DNA damage checkpoints and shortened telomeres (Allsopp et al., 1992; Bridger and Kill, 2004; Goldman et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2005, 2006; Decker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and confirmed by telomere blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Critically shortened telomeres elicit a DNA damage response and trigger senescence, resulting in irreversible growth arrest.
source: Critically shortened telomeres elicit a DNA damage response and trigger senescence, resulting in irreversible growth arrest (d'Adda di Fagagna et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Ectopic expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) extends the proliferative capacity of HGPS fibroblasts.
source: Previous results revealed that ectopic expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) extends the proliferative capacity of HGPS fibroblasts and rescues progerin-induced DNA damage (Kudlow et al., 2008; Benson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and confirmed by growth curve data in Figure 1C.

claim: Ectopic expression of TERT rescues progerin-induced DNA damage.
source: Previous results revealed that ectopic expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) extends the proliferative capacity of HGPS fibroblasts and rescues progerin-induced DNA damage (Kudlow et al., 2008; Benson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and confirmed by 53BP1 foci data in Figure 1D.

claim: Progerin leads to increased DNA damage in primary human fibroblasts.
source: Here, we describe a regulatable cellular model of progeria and show that upon induction in primary human fibroblasts, progerin leads to increased DNA damage, cellular senescence, senescence-associated reduction of lamin B1, nuclear morphology defects and altered expression of H3K27me3, in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by 53BP1 foci quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: Progerin leads to cellular senescence in primary human fibroblasts.
source: Here, we describe a regulatable cellular model of progeria and show that upon induction in primary human fibroblasts, progerin leads to increased DNA damage, cellular senescence, senescence-associated reduction of lamin B1, nuclear morphology defects and altered expression of H3K27me3, in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Progerin leads to senescence-associated reduction of lamin B1 in primary human fibroblasts.
source: Here, we describe a regulatable cellular model of progeria and show that upon induction in primary human fibroblasts, progerin leads to increased DNA damage, cellular senescence, senescence-associated reduction of lamin B1, nuclear morphology defects and altered expression of H3K27me3, in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Progerin leads to nuclear morphology defects in primary human fibroblasts.
source: Here, we describe a regulatable cellular model of progeria and show that upon induction in primary human fibroblasts, progerin leads to increased DNA damage, cellular senescence, senescence-associated reduction of lamin B1, nuclear morphology defects and altered expression of H3K27me3, in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Progerin leads to altered expression of H3K27me3 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Here, we describe a regulatable cellular model of progeria and show that upon induction in primary human fibroblasts, progerin leads to increased DNA damage, cellular senescence, senescence-associated reduction of lamin B1, nuclear morphology defects and altered expression of H3K27me3, in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot analysis in Figure 1E showing inverse correlation between progerin and H3K27me3 levels.

claim: Exogenous TERT prevents the proliferative defects induced by progerin.
source: Exogenous TERT prevents the proliferative defects, DNA damage, lamin B1 reduction and gene expression differences induced by progerin, although nuclear morphology defects and altered deposition of H3K27me3 are not prevented by TERT.
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 1C showing no proliferation defects in TERT+ cells expressing progerin.

claim: Exogenous TERT prevents DNA damage induced by progerin.
source: Exogenous TERT prevents the proliferative defects, DNA damage, lamin B1 reduction and gene expression differences induced by progerin, although nuclear morphology defects and altered deposition of H3K27me3 are not prevented by TERT.
evidence: This is supported by 53BP1 foci data in Figure 1D showing reduced DNA damage in TERT+ cells.

claim: Exogenous TERT prevents lamin B1 reduction induced by progerin.
source: Exogenous TERT prevents the proliferative defects, DNA damage, lamin B1 reduction and gene expression differences induced by progerin, although nuclear morphology defects and altered deposition of H3K27me3 are not prevented by TERT.
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Exogenous TERT prevents gene expression differences induced by progerin.
source: Exogenous TERT prevents the proliferative defects, DNA damage, lamin B1 reduction and gene expression differences induced by progerin, although nuclear morphology defects and altered deposition of H3K27me3 are not prevented by TERT.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data in Figure 1H showing restored gene expression profile in TERT+ cells.

claim: Nuclear morphology defects induced by progerin are not prevented by TERT.
source: Exogenous TERT prevents the proliferative defects, DNA damage, lamin B1 reduction and gene expression differences induced by progerin, although nuclear morphology defects and altered deposition of H3K27me3 are not prevented by TERT.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing persistent nuclear abnormalities in TERT+HGPS cells.

claim: Altered deposition of H3K27me3 induced by progerin is not prevented by TERT.
source: Exogenous TERT prevents the proliferative defects, DNA damage, lamin B1 reduction and gene expression differences induced by progerin, although nuclear morphology defects and altered deposition of H3K27me3 are not prevented by TERT.
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot analysis in Figure 1E showing inverse correlation between progerin and H3K27me3 in both TERT-negative and TERT+ cells.

claim: Progerin inhibits proliferation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: To test this, we expressed increasing levels of progerin in primary and TERT+ fibroblasts by increasing the concentration of DOX (0–2000 ng/ml). This resulted in progerin inhibiting the proliferation of primary fibroblasts in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data in Figure 1C showing decreased proliferation with increasing DOX concentrations.

claim: Defective proliferation induced by progerin is accompanied by a gradual increase in DNA damage levels.
source: Defective proliferation was accompanied by a gradual increase in DNA damage levels, as quantified by the number of 53BP1 foci per nucleus (Figure 1D, left panel, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by 53BP1 foci quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: Progerin must reach a threshold of approximately 30-40% of endogenous lamin A levels to induce DNA damage and inhibit proliferation.
source: The levels of progerin required to induce a phenotype corresponded to ∼30–40% of endogenous lamin A levels (at 100–250 ng/ml DOX; Figure 1B–D). Progerin therefore must reach a certain threshold to induce DNA damage and inhibit proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from western blot data in Figure 1B and phenotypic data in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: There is an inverse correlation between progerin and H3K27me3 levels in single cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, a scatterplot analysis of >9800 nuclei revealed an inverse correlation between progerin and H3K27me3 levels (Pearson r = −0.43 and −0.24 for TERT negative and TERT+ cells expressing progerin, respectively, p < 0.001, Figure 1E, inset).
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot analysis in Figure 1E with statistical correlation analysis.

claim: Progerin mediated loss of H3K27me3 is not prevented by TERT.
source: However, progerin mediated loss of H3K27me3 was not prevented by TERT.
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot data in Figure 1E showing inverse correlation in both TERT-negative and TERT+ cells.

claim: The inverse correlation between progerin expression and loss of H3K27me3 is apparent in two primary HGPS cell lines.
source: The inverse correlation between progerin expression and loss of H3K27me3 is also apparent in two primary HGPS cell lines (Figure 1F, Pearson r = −0.70 and −0.52 for HGPS 01972 and HGPS 11513 respectively, p < 0.001), as well as in one TERT+HGPS cell line (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K, Pearson r = −0.5).
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot analysis in Figure 1F with statistical correlation analysis.

claim: The expression of 142 genes was increased or decreased more than twofold in progerin vs lamin A expressing cells.
source: The expression of 142 genes was increased or decreased more than twofold in progerin vs lamin A expressing cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by microarray analysis data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Many gene expression changes induced by progerin are associated with senescence.
source: Many of these gene expression changes were associated with senescence, including a reduction of Wnt2 (Ye et al., 2007), increased expression of matrix metalloproteinases (Kang et al., 2003) and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) (Kortlever et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data and citations to published research on senescence markers.

claim: Expression of TERT prevented nearly all gene expression changes induced by progerin.
source: Expression of TERT prevented nearly all these changes in the differentially expressed genes, and restored the gene expression profile to that seen in cells not expressing progerin (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap data in Figure 1H showing similar gene expression patterns between TERT+ progerin cells and non-progerin controls.

claim: Expression of exogenous progerin or lamin A does not impair the proliferation of pluripotent ESCs.
source: Expression of the exogenous progerin or lamin A did not impair the proliferation of the pluripotent ESCs (Figure 2A), induce significant changes in gene expression (Figure 2B), alter nuclear lamina structure, as measured by lamin B1 and emerin expression, nor affect the expression of the pluripotency markers Nanog, Oct-4 and Sox-2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression of exogenous progerin or lamin A does not induce significant changes in gene expression in ESCs.
source: Expression of the exogenous progerin or lamin A did not impair the proliferation of the pluripotent ESCs (Figure 2A), induce significant changes in gene expression (Figure 2B), alter nuclear lamina structure, as measured by lamin B1 and emerin expression, nor affect the expression of the pluripotency markers Nanog, Oct-4 and Sox-2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap data in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of exogenous progerin or lamin A does not alter nuclear lamina structure in ESCs.
source: Expression of the exogenous progerin or lamin A did not impair the proliferation of the pluripotent ESCs (Figure 2A), induce significant changes in gene expression (Figure 2B), alter nuclear lamina structure, as measured by lamin B1 and emerin expression, nor affect the expression of the pluripotency markers Nanog, Oct-4 and Sox-2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of exogenous progerin or lamin A does not affect the expression of pluripotency markers in ESCs.
source: Expression of the exogenous progerin or lamin A did not impair the proliferation of the pluripotent ESCs (Figure 2A), induce significant changes in gene expression (Figure 2B), alter nuclear lamina structure, as measured by lamin B1 and emerin expression, nor affect the expression of the pluripotency markers Nanog, Oct-4 and Sox-2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data in Figure 2C.

claim: TERT is expressed in undifferentiated ESC, but is repressed during differentiation.
source: TERT is expressed in undifferentiated ESC, but is repressed during differentiation (Armstrong et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The EB outgrowth of differentiated cells is significantly reduced in progerin expressing cells.
source: While the total EB size did not vary significantly between the different conditions (Figure 2E), the EB outgrowth of differentiated cells was significantly reduced in progerin expressing cells (Figure 2F, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 2F.

claim: Expression of progerin in Tert−/− ESC leads to a reduction in cell number.
source: Expression of progerin in Tert−/− ESC led to a reduction in cell number (Figure 2G), rapidly induced differentiation and significantly impaired ability of ESC to form embryoid bodies (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data in Figure 2G.

claim: Expression of progerin in Tert−/− ESC rapidly induces differentiation.
source: Expression of progerin in Tert−/− ESC led to a reduction in cell number (Figure 2G), rapidly induced differentiation and significantly impaired ability of ESC to form embryoid bodies (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is supported by brightfield microscopy images in Figure 2H.

claim: Expression of progerin in Tert−/− ESC significantly impairs ability to form embryoid bodies.
source: Expression of progerin in Tert−/− ESC led to a reduction in cell number (Figure 2G), rapidly induced differentiation and significantly impaired ability of ESC to form embryoid bodies (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is supported by EB size quantification in Figure 2I.

claim: Physiological expression levels of TERT are necessary and sufficient to prevent progerin-induced defects.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that physiological expression levels of TERT are necessary and sufficient to prevent progerin-induced defects.
evidence: This is inferred from ESC experiments showing protection in wild-type ESC but not in Tert−/− ESC (Figures 2A-I).

claim: A previous report indicated that LAP2α may directly interact with chromatin and telomeres.
source: However, a previous report indicated that LAP2α may directly interact with chromatin and telomeres (Dechat et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: In normal nuclei, LAP2α is present as discrete foci distributed throughout the nucleoplasm.
source: In normal nuclei, LAP2α was present as discrete foci distributed throughout the nucleoplasm (Figure 4A,B), with many foci closely localized with telomeres, visualized by staining for TRF1, a component of the telomere-associated shelterin complex (De Lange, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM microscopy images in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Many LAP2α foci are closely localized with telomeres in normal nuclei.
source: In normal nuclei, LAP2α was present as discrete foci distributed throughout the nucleoplasm (Figure 4A,B), with many foci closely localized with telomeres, visualized by staining for TRF1, a component of the telomere-associated shelterin complex (De Lange, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM microscopy images in Figure 4A,B and distribution profile in Figure 4D.

claim: In normal nuclei, the highest average LAP2α signal intensity is within approximately 200 nm of each telomere.
source: We found that in normal nuclei, the highest average LAP2α signal intensity is within ∼200 nm of each telomere.
evidence: This is supported by intensity profile analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: In HGPS nuclei, the distribution of LAP2α in relation to the telomeres is significantly altered.
source: In contrast, in HGPS nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), the distribution of LAP2α in relation to the telomeres was significantly altered, and reached its maximum value roughly 360–400 nm from the center of each telomere (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by intensity profile analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: In HGPS nuclei, LAP2α reaches its maximum value roughly 360-400 nm from the center of each telomere.
source: In contrast, in HGPS nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), the distribution of LAP2α in relation to the telomeres was significantly altered, and reached its maximum value roughly 360–400 nm from the center of each telomere (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by intensity profile analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: The close physical proximity between LAP2α and telomeres is disrupted in HGPS nuclei.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that the close physical proximity between LAP2α and telomeres is disrupted in HGPS nuclei.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple analyses including intensity profiles (Figure 4D) and co-localization quantification (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Approximately 50% of telomeres localize to within 250 nm of the nuclear lamina in interphase nuclei.
source: We found that ∼50% of the telomeres localized to within 250 nm of the nuclear lamina in interphase nuclei, but we did not observe any change in telomere distribution between normal- and HGPS+TERT fibroblasts (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM quantification data in Figure 4E.

claim: There is no change in telomere distribution between normal and HGPS+TERT fibroblasts.
source: We found that ∼50% of the telomeres localized to within 250 nm of the nuclear lamina in interphase nuclei, but we did not observe any change in telomere distribution between normal- and HGPS+TERT fibroblasts (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM quantification data in Figure 4E.

claim: Progerin expression or mis-localization of LAP2α does not affect telomere distribution within the nucleus.
source: This suggests that progerin expression or mis-localization of LAP2α does not affect telomere distribution within the nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that telomere distribution is unchanged in HGPS cells (Figure 4E).

claim: LAP2 depletion enhances proliferation of primary and TERT+ fibroblasts.
source: First, we depleted the α, β and γ isoforms of LAP2 using lentiviral delivered shRNA, and observed, in agreement with previous reports, enhanced proliferation of primary and TERT+ fibroblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C) (Dorner et al., 2006; Naetar et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and citations to published research.

claim: Loss of LAP2 enhances progerin-induced proliferation defects.
source: Surprisingly, and in contrast to normal cells, the loss of LAP2 enhanced progerin-induced proliferation defects (Figure 5C, red arrowhead).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5A (note: text refers to Figure 5C but likely means 5A based on context).

claim: The enhanced reduction in proliferation caused by LAP2 depletion in progerin-expressing cells is rescued by TERT expression.
source: However, this enhanced reduction in proliferation was rescued by TERT expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: LAP2 depletion potentiates the detrimental effect of progerin on cell proliferation.
source: From these findings we conclude that LAP2 depletion potentiates the detrimental effect of progerin on cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LAP2 depletion enhances progerin-induced proliferation defects (Figure 5A).

claim: Increased expression of LAP2α impairs cell proliferation in a dose-dependent manner in normal cells.
source: In normal cells, increased expression of LAP2α impairs cell proliferation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G), as previously reported (Dorner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and citation to published research.

claim: A moderate increase in LAP2α levels almost completely restores the proliferative capacity of cells expressing progerin.
source: Strikingly, a moderate increase in LAP2α levels almost completely restored the proliferative capacity of cells expressing progerin (Figure 5C, red arrowhead), reduced the number of cells with DNA damage foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and prevented premature senescence in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5C.

claim: Increased LAP2α levels reduce the number of cells with DNA damage foci in progerin-expressing cells.
source: Strikingly, a moderate increase in LAP2α levels almost completely restored the proliferative capacity of cells expressing progerin (Figure 5C, red arrowhead), reduced the number of cells with DNA damage foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and prevented premature senescence in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by 53BP1 foci quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Increased LAP2α levels prevent premature senescence in progerin-expressing cells.
source: Strikingly, a moderate increase in LAP2α levels almost completely restored the proliferative capacity of cells expressing progerin (Figure 5C, red arrowhead), reduced the number of cells with DNA damage foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and prevented premature senescence in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Increased LAP2α impairs proliferation in wild-type cells.
source: This is in contrast to wild-type cells (or vector control cells), in which increased LAP2α impaired proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G) and increased premature senescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Expression of LAP2α in progerin expressing cells increases H3K27me3 levels compared to non-induced controls.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, expression of LAP2α in progerin expressing cells increased H3K27me3 levels as compared to non-induced controls (n = 3, p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by box plot analysis in Figure 5F.

claim: Overexpression of LAP2α in TERT+HGPS fibroblasts results in a significant increase in H3K27me3.
source: Scatterplot analysis of ≈5500 nuclei revealed a significant increase in H3K27me3 upon induction of LAP2α (Pearson r = 0.1835, p < 0.01) (n = 3, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot analysis in Figure 5G.

claim: Overexpression of LAP2α does not ameliorate progerin induced nuclear abnormalities in TERT+HGPS fibroblasts.
source: However, overexpression of LAP2α did not ameliorate progerin induced nuclear abnormalities in TERT+HGPS fibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Overexpression of LAP2α in wild type cells not expressing progerin does not result in a significant increase in H3K27me3 levels.
source: Lastly, overexpression of LAP2α in wild type cells, not expressing progerin, did not result in a significant increase in H3K27me3 levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by box plot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Increasing LAP2α levels prevents progerin-induced proliferation defects and alleviates the progerin-induced reduction in the heterochromatin mark H3K27me3.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that increasing LAP2α levels prevents progerin-induced proliferation defects and alleviates the progerin-induced reduction in the heterochromatin mark H3K27me3.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments showing rescue of proliferation (Figure 5C) and increased H3K27me3 (Figures 5F,G).

claim: A reduction in heterochromatin renders DNA vulnerable to increased damage.
source: A reduction in heterochromatin renders DNA vulnerable to increased damage (Di Micco et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Valproic acid treatment exacerbates progerin-induced proliferation defects at concentrations that have no discernible effect on non-induced wild type cells.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, valproic acid treatment exacerbated progerin-induced proliferation defects, at concentrations that had no discernible effect on non-induced wild type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: A reduction in heterochromatin may render cells more susceptible to progerin-induced proliferation defects.
source: Based on these results we speculate that a reduction in heterochromatin may render cells more susceptible to progerin-induced proliferation defects.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on valproic acid experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: Ectopic expression of LAP2β leads to a reduction in the rate of proliferation in both normal and progerin expressing fibroblasts.
source: In contrast to LAP2α, ectopic expression of LAP2β led to a reduction in the rate of proliferation in both normal and progerin expressing fibroblasts (Figure 5H, red arrow).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5H.

claim: Expression of the α-isoform of LAP2 specifically ameliorates progerin-induced proliferation defects and increases the levels of heterochromatin associated H3K27me3.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that expression of the α-isoform of LAP2 specifically ameliorates progerin-induced proliferation defects and increases the levels of heterochromatin associated H3K27me3.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing LAP2α rescue effects (Figures 5C,F,G) with LAP2β effects (Figure 5H).

claim: Progerin inhibits proliferation, causes DNA damage and entry into senescence in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: By using this system, we find that progerin inhibits proliferation, causes DNA damage and entry into senescence in a dose-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Progerin's detrimental effects become apparent only when levels reach a critical threshold.
source: These results suggest that progerin's detrimental effects become apparent only when levels reach a critical threshold.
evidence: This is inferred from dose-response experiments showing effects at 30-40% of endogenous lamin A levels.

claim: Tissues expressing relatively high levels of lamin A/progerin are central to the pathology of HGPS.
source: This provides a compelling explanation as to why tissues expressing relatively high levels of lamin A/progerin are central to the pathology of HGPS (Jung et al., 2012; Nissan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from dose-dependent effects and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Ectopic expression of TERT prevents progerin-induced DNA damage, proliferation defects, premature senescence and senescence-associated loss of lamin B1.
source: Our results confirm that ectopic expression of TERT prevents progerin-induced DNA damage, proliferation defects, premature senescence and senescence-associated loss of lamin B1 (Kudlow et al., 2008; Benson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to published research.

claim: Physiological levels of TERT are sufficient to prevent progerin-induced proliferation defects and changes in gene expression.
source: Moreover, by expressing progerin and lamin A in ESCs which express endogenous levels of TERT, and Tert−/− ESC, we demonstrate that physiological levels of TERT are sufficient to prevent progerin-induced proliferation defects and changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by ESC experiments in Figures 2A-I.

claim: TERT expression during embryogenesis or in adult stem cell compartments may protect these cells from the detrimental consequences of progerin.
source: These results may be relevant to HGPS patients, as TERT expression during embryogenesis or in adult stem cell compartments may protect these cells from the detrimental consequences of progerin (Wright et al., 1996).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on ESC experiments and supported by citation.

claim: HGPS may be quite different from dyskeratosis congenita (DC), a premature ageing disorder that is caused by defects in telomerase that particularly affects stem cell maintenance.
source: In this respect, HGPS may be quite different from dyskeratosis congenita (DC), a premature ageing disorder that is caused by defects in telomerase that particularly affects stem cell maintenance (Vulliamy et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TERT protects against progerin effects and supported by citation about DC.

claim: TERT does not prevent progerin-induced loss of heterochromatin.
source: However in determining the levels of the heterochromatin marker H3K27me3, in primary and TERT-positive cells, we found that TERT does not prevent progerin-induced loss of heterochromatin.
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot data in Figure 1E showing inverse correlation in both TERT-negative and TERT+ cells.

claim: The changes in gene expression in primary fibroblasts expressing progerin are a consequence of premature senescence, rather than a direct consequence of progerin expression.
source: This, in turn, suggests that the changes in gene expression in primary fibroblasts expressing progerin are a consequence of premature senescence, rather than a direct consequence of progerin expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TERT prevents gene expression changes (Figure 1H) but not H3K27me3 loss (Figure 1E).

claim: The physical interaction between LAP2α and progerin is significantly reduced compared to lamin A.
source: Our interactome analysis confirmed this interaction, but demonstrated that the physical interaction between LAP2α and progerin was significantly reduced.
evidence: This is supported by BioID analysis (Figure 3C) and co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 3D).

claim: A significant proportion of telomeres can be found at the nuclear periphery.
source: We found that a significant proportion of telomeres can be found at the nuclear periphery, and that their distribution is not perturbed by progerin.
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM quantification in Figure 4E.

claim: Telomere distribution is not perturbed by progerin.
source: We found that a significant proportion of telomeres can be found at the nuclear periphery, and that their distribution is not perturbed by progerin.
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM quantification in Figure 4E showing no change between WT and HGPS.

claim: Other progeroid mutations (LMNA E145K), or loss of LMNA may have different effects on telomere localization.
source: This suggests that other progeroid mutations (LMNA E145K), or loss of LMNA may have different effects on telomere localization (Gonzalez-Suarez et al., 2009; Taimen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that progerin does not affect telomere distribution, contrasting with cited studies on other mutations.

claim: The association of LAP2α with telomeres is reduced in HGPS.
source: Although telomere distribution was unaffected, we find that the association of LAP2α with telomeres is reduced in HGPS.
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM analysis in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Depletion of LAP2 exacerbates the progerin-induced defects.
source: Depletion of LAP2 exacerbated the progerin-induced defects whereas increasing nuclear LAP2α levels prevented the proliferation defects, DNA damage and premature senescence resulting from progerin expression.
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing nuclear LAP2α levels prevents the proliferation defects, DNA damage and premature senescence resulting from progerin expression.
source: Depletion of LAP2 exacerbated the progerin-induced defects whereas increasing nuclear LAP2α levels prevented the proliferation defects, DNA damage and premature senescence resulting from progerin expression.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The rescue of progerin-induced defects is specific to the α-isoform of LAP2.
source: This rescue was specific to the α-isoform of LAP2, as increasing LAP2β levels failed to restore normal rates of proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by comparing LAP2α effects (Figure 5C) with LAP2β effects (Figure 5H).

claim: Increased or decreased levels of LAP2α lead to diametrically opposed effects between normal and progerin-expressing cells.
source: Moreover, increased or decreased levels of LAP2α led to diametrically opposed effects between normal and progerin-expressing cells.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing effects in normal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) versus progerin-expressing cells (Figure 5C).

claim: LAP2α plays a key role in the HGPS pathophysiology.
source: Taken together, our data provide mechanistic evidence that LAP2α plays a key role in the HGPS pathophysiology and that progerin-induced defects are rescued by ectopic expression of LAP2α.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments showing impaired LAP2α-progerin interaction and rescue by LAP2α overexpression.

claim: Progerin-induced defects are rescued by ectopic expression of LAP2α.
source: Taken together, our data provide mechanistic evidence that LAP2α plays a key role in the HGPS pathophysiology and that progerin-induced defects are rescued by ectopic expression of LAP2α.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5C,F,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Changes in the levels of LAP2α are emerging as a consistent feature in at least some of the laminopathies.
source: Changes in the levels of LAP2α are emerging as a consistent feature in at least some of the laminopathies.
evidence: This is inferred from the current study and cited research on other laminopathies.

claim: Loss of Lmna, that causes cardiomyopathy and muscular wasting/dystrophy results in a transient increase in LAP2α in muscle precursors and myoblasts.
source: Loss of Lmna, that causes cardiomyopathy and muscular wasting/dystrophy results in a transient increase in LAP2α in muscle precursors and myoblasts (Melcon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Ablation of LAP2α in Lmna null mice significantly reduces the severity of the disease and increases longevity.
source: However, ablation of LAP2α in Lmna null mice significantly reduces the severity of the disease and increases longevity (Cohen et al., 2013), a result similar to that observed following elimination of another nuclear envelope protein Sun1 (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The lamina/nuclear envelope forms an integrated and mutually regulated stoichiometric network of proteins.
source: Together these observations, and those presented here, suggest that the lamina/nuclear envelope forms an integrated and mutually regulated stoichiometric network of proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from observations about LAP2α changes in various laminopathies.

claim: When the lamina/nuclear envelope network is disrupted by LMNA mutations, one of the consequences is that the levels of other protein components change, with this change being a major contributing factor to the consequent pathology.
source: When the network is disrupted, for example by LMNA mutations, one of the consequences is that the levels of other protein components change, with this change being a major contributing factor to the consequent pathology.
evidence: This is inferred from the current study and cited research on laminopathies.

claim: In normal cells, telomeres are surrounded by LAP2α complexes, which in turn interact with nuclear lamins.
source: Within this context, and based on the results presented here, we propose a model linking progerin and LAP2α to human telomeres (Figure 6). In this model, telomeres in normal cells are surrounded by LAP2α complexes, which in turn interact with nuclear lamins (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data showing LAP2α localization near telomeres (Figure 4) and LAP2α-lamin A interaction (Figure 3).

claim: In progeria, the impaired association between LAP2α and progerin disrupts telomere organization and ultimately leads to premature senescence.
source: In progeria, the impaired association between LAP2α and progerin disrupts this organization and ultimately leads to premature senescence (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data showing impaired LAP2α-progerin interaction (Figure 3) and altered LAP2α-telomere association (Figure 4).

claim: Premature senescence in progeria can be prevented by expression of either telomerase or by increasing the levels of LAP2α.
source: This can be prevented by expression of either telomerase or by increasing the levels of LAP2α (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue by TERT (Figure 1) and LAP2α (Figure 5).

claim: The effect of TERT mechanistically differs from the rescue by LAP2α.
source: However, it is not clear if the effect of TERT mechanistically differs from the rescue by LAP2α. Our data suggest that this indeed might be the case: in contrast to LAP2α, TERT expression does not ameliorate the progerin-induced reduction in H3K27me3 levels.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing TERT effects (Figure 1E) with LAP2α effects (Figures 5F,G) on H3K27me3.

claim: TERT expression does not ameliorate the progerin-induced reduction in H3K27me3 levels.
source: Our data suggest that this indeed might be the case: in contrast to LAP2α, TERT expression does not ameliorate the progerin-induced reduction in H3K27me3 levels.
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot data in Figure 1E.

claim: Telomeres are fragile sites and a reduction in heterochromatin has been associated with increased susceptibility to DNA damage and cell cycle arrest.
source: Telomeres are fragile sites and a reduction in heterochromatin has been associated with increased susceptibility to DNA damage and cell cycle arrest (Sfeir et al., 2009; Di Micco et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Progerin expression destabilizes chromosome ends, causing DNA damage and premature senescence.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, progerin expression destabilizes chromosome ends, causing DNA damage and premature senescence (Benson et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and confirmed by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: By elongating telomeres, TERT counteracts telomere loss and prevents the telomeric DNA damage associated with HGPS.
source: By elongating telomeres, TERT counteracts such telomere loss and prevents the telomeric DNA damage associated with HGPS (Figure 6E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J) (Kudlow et al., 2008; Benson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by telomere blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) and citations to published research.

claim: Increased LAP2α alleviates the progerin-induced loss of H3K27me3.
source: In contrast to TERT, we found that increased LAP2α alleviates the progerin-induced loss of H3K27me3 (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: Increased LAP2α stabilizes chromatin structure by increasing H3K27me3 and prevents progerin-associated DNA damage that results in premature senescence.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that increased LAP2α stabilizes chromatin structure by increasing H3K27me3 and prevents progerin-associated DNA damage that resulted in premature senescence (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experiments showing LAP2α increases H3K27me3 (Figures 5F,G) and reduces DNA damage (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Both LAP2α and H3K27me3 decline during normal ageing in human cells.
source: In support of this notion, both LAP2α and H3K27me3 decline during normal ageing in human cells (Scaffidi and Misteli, 2006; Naetar et al., 2007; Dreesen et al., 2013), and it has been suggested that sustaining heterochromatin levels may extend lifespan by protecting against DNA damage (Larson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Sustaining heterochromatin levels may extend lifespan by protecting against DNA damage.
source: In support of this notion, both LAP2α and H3K27me3 decline during normal ageing in human cells (Scaffidi and Misteli, 2006; Naetar et al., 2007; Dreesen et al., 2013), and it has been suggested that sustaining heterochromatin levels may extend lifespan by protecting against DNA damage (Larson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: HGPS patients appear normal at birth, but by 12-18 months begin to exhibit features associated with accelerated ageing.
source: HGPS patients appear normal at birth, but by 12–18 months begin to exhibit features associated with accelerated ageing, and usually die in their teens due to cardiovascular failure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HGPS clinical presentation.

claim: HGPS patients usually die in their teens due to cardiovascular failure.
source: HGPS patients appear normal at birth, but by 12–18 months begin to exhibit features associated with accelerated ageing, and usually die in their teens due to cardiovascular failure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HGPS clinical presentation.

claim: The nuclear lamina is a proteinaceous meshwork consisting of A-type and B-type lamins.
source: The nuclear lamina, a proteinaceous meshwork consisting of A-type and B-type lamins, underlies the inner nuclear membrane and is important for maintaining interphase nuclear architecture.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nuclear lamina structure.

claim: The nuclear lamina underlies the inner nuclear membrane and is important for maintaining interphase nuclear architecture.
source: The nuclear lamina, a proteinaceous meshwork consisting of A-type and B-type lamins, underlies the inner nuclear membrane and is important for maintaining interphase nuclear architecture.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nuclear lamina function.

claim: The nuclear lamina provides a structural scaffold for factors involved in DNA repair, replication and transcription.
source: In addition, it provides a structural scaffold for factors involved in DNA repair, replication and transcription (Burke and Stewart, 2006; Dechat et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Mutations in the LMNA gene are responsible for a variety of human genetic disorders, collectively called the laminopathies.
source: Mutations in the LMNA gene are responsible for a variety of human genetic disorders, collectively called the laminopathies (Burke and Stewart, 2006; Worman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Laminopathies include forms of muscular dystrophy, cardiomyopathy, lipodystrophy and the premature aging disease, Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS).
source: Laminopathies include forms of muscular dystrophy, cardiomyopathy, lipodystrophy and the premature aging disease, Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about laminopathies.
